claim: The mouse visual system is increasingly being used as a model system for studying cortical sensory processing.
source: The mouse visual system is increasingly (Baker, 2013; Priebe and McGee, 2014) being used as a model system for studying both cortical sensory processing (Glickfeld et al., 2013, 2014; Niell and Stryker, 2008, 2010; Wang et al., 2011a) and behavior (Busse et al., 2011; Harvey et al., 2012; Histed et al., 2012; Hoy et al., 2016; Montijn et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature on mouse visual system studies.

claim: The mouse visual system is increasingly being used as a model system for studying behavior.
source: The mouse visual system is increasingly (Baker, 2013; Priebe and McGee, 2014) being used as a model system for studying both cortical sensory processing (Glickfeld et al., 2013, 2014; Niell and Stryker, 2008, 2010; Wang et al., 2011a) and behavior (Busse et al., 2011; Harvey et al., 2012; Histed et al., 2012; Hoy et al., 2016; Montijn et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature on mouse behavioral studies.

claim: Most physiological work in mouse vision has used achromatic stimuli.
source: While most physiological work has used achromatic stimuli (Durand et al., 2016; Niell and Stryker, 2008), mice, like most other mammals, display physiological color-opponent signals in the retina (Baden et al., 2013; Baden et al., 2016; Breuninger et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016), through LGN (Denman et al., 2017) and possibly V1 (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published physiological studies.

claim: Mice display physiological color-opponent signals in the retina.
source: While most physiological work has used achromatic stimuli (Durand et al., 2016; Niell and Stryker, 2008), mice, like most other mammals, display physiological color-opponent signals in the retina (Baden et al., 2013; Baden et al., 2016; Breuninger et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016), through LGN (Denman et al., 2017) and possibly V1 (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies demonstrating color-opponent signals in mouse retina.

claim: Mice display physiological color-opponent signals through LGN.
source: While most physiological work has used achromatic stimuli (Durand et al., 2016; Niell and Stryker, 2008), mice, like most other mammals, display physiological color-opponent signals in the retina (Baden et al., 2013; Baden et al., 2016; Breuninger et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016), through LGN (Denman et al., 2017) and possibly V1 (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on LGN color-opponent signals.

claim: Mice possibly display physiological color-opponent signals in V1.
source: While most physiological work has used achromatic stimuli (Durand et al., 2016; Niell and Stryker, 2008), mice, like most other mammals, display physiological color-opponent signals in the retina (Baden et al., 2013; Baden et al., 2016; Breuninger et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016), through LGN (Denman et al., 2017) and possibly V1 (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study suggesting V1 color-opponent signals, with uncertainty indicated by 'possibly'.

claim: The mouse retina displays asymmetric and mixed expression of its two opsins along the dorsal-ventral axis.
source: The mouse retina displays asymmetric and mixed expression of its two opsins along the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina, creating opposing gradients of short and middle opsins (Applebury et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2011b) and resulting in gradients of wavelength-band-specific responses (Chang et al., 2013; Denman et al., 2017; Rhim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on opsin expression patterns.

claim: The mouse retina has opposing gradients of short and middle opsins.
source: The mouse retina displays asymmetric and mixed expression of its two opsins along the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina, creating opposing gradients of short and middle opsins (Applebury et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2011b) and resulting in gradients of wavelength-band-specific responses (Chang et al., 2013; Denman et al., 2017; Rhim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on opsin gradients.

claim: Opposing gradients of short and middle opsins result in gradients of wavelength-band-specific responses.
source: The mouse retina displays asymmetric and mixed expression of its two opsins along the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina, creating opposing gradients of short and middle opsins (Applebury et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2011b) and resulting in gradients of wavelength-band-specific responses (Chang et al., 2013; Denman et al., 2017; Rhim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies demonstrating wavelength-specific response gradients.

claim: The substrate for cone-driven color-opponent signals exists only in the overlapping 'opsin transition zone'.
source: Therefore, the substrate for cone-driven color-opponent signals, and any color sensitivity, exists only in the overlapping 'opsin transition zone' (Baden et al., 2013; Denman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies and logical inference from opsin distribution patterns.

claim: Short and middle opsin responses broadly overlap in V1 and higher visual areas.
source: However, short and middle opsin responses broadly overlap in V1 and higher visual areas (Rhim et al., 2017) and rod-cone antagonism can also create color opponency in some mouse retinal ganglion cells (Joesch and Meister, 2016), presenting the possibility that behaviorally relevant color information could be extracted more broadly across retinotopic space.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on V1 and higher visual area responses.

claim: Rod-cone antagonism can create color opponency in some mouse retinal ganglion cells.
source: However, short and middle opsin responses broadly overlap in V1 and higher visual areas (Rhim et al., 2017) and rod-cone antagonism can also create color opponency in some mouse retinal ganglion cells (Joesch and Meister, 2016), presenting the possibility that behaviorally relevant color information could be extracted more broadly across retinotopic space.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on rod-cone antagonism.

claim: Behaviorally relevant color information could potentially be extracted more broadly across retinotopic space than the opsin transition zone alone.
source: However, short and middle opsin responses broadly overlap in V1 and higher visual areas (Rhim et al., 2017) and rod-cone antagonism can also create color opponency in some mouse retinal ganglion cells (Joesch and Meister, 2016), presenting the possibility that behaviorally relevant color information could be extracted more broadly across retinotopic space.
evidence: Speculative claim based on inference from cited physiological findings.

claim: There is some evidence for color discrimination in mice.
source: There is some evidence for color discrimination (Jacobs et al., 2004), but it remains unclear how this depends on overall luminance, luminance contrast, or retinotopic position.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on mouse color discrimination.

claim: It remains unclear how mouse color discrimination depends on overall luminance, luminance contrast, or retinotopic position.
source: There is some evidence for color discrimination (Jacobs et al., 2004), but it remains unclear how this depends on overall luminance, luminance contrast, or retinotopic position.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: It is not known if the gradients in opsin distribution lead to variations in behavioral luminance sensitivity across space.
source: Further, it is not known if the gradients in opsin distribution lead to variations in behavioral luminance sensitivity across space.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: Non-uniformity in luminance sensitivity would impact studies of visuotopically extended V1 populations.
source: Such non-uniformity would impact studies of visuotopically extended V1 populations, such as studies of population sparsity (Froudarakis et al., 2014), population correlations (Montijn et al., 2016a) and other notions of population coding (Montijn et al., 2015; Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: Logical inference about the implications of non-uniform sensitivity, with citations to relevant studies.

claim: The study measured detectability of luminance and color changes separately across elevation spanning ~75°.
source: By measuring detectability of luminance and color changes separately across elevation (spanning ~75°), we are able to generate an estimate of wavelength-specific contrast sensitivity across visual space.
evidence: Description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Mice were able to discriminate color.
source: Mice were able to discriminate color, but only at elevations above the horizon.
evidence: Primary finding from the behavioral experiments reported in the study.

claim: Mice were able to discriminate color only at elevations above the horizon.
source: Mice were able to discriminate color, but only at elevations above the horizon.
evidence: Primary finding from the behavioral experiments reported in the study.

claim: Mice were able to discriminate color more broadly across visuotopic space than expected from the cone-opsin distribution.
source: We found that mice were able to discriminate color and were able to do so more broadly across visuotopic space than expected from the cone-opsin distribution.
evidence: Primary finding from the behavioral experiments compared to predictions from opsin distribution.

claim: Wavelength-band-specific differences in luminance sensitivity were found.
source: We also found wavelength-band-specific differences in luminance sensitivity.
evidence: Primary finding from the behavioral experiments reported in the study.

claim: Both wavelength-specific luminance and color contrast sensitivity are dependent on retinotopic location.
source: We find both wavelength-specific luminance and color contrast sensitivity to be dependent on retinotopic location, but that these differences in sensitivity were less dramatic than expected from the cone opsin distribution, suggesting behavioral access to differential activation of rods and cones.
evidence: Primary finding from the behavioral experiments reported in the study.

claim: Differences in wavelength-specific luminance and color contrast sensitivity were less dramatic than expected from the cone opsin distribution.
source: We find both wavelength-specific luminance and color contrast sensitivity to be dependent on retinotopic location, but that these differences in sensitivity were less dramatic than expected from the cone opsin distribution, suggesting behavioral access to differential activation of rods and cones.
evidence: Primary finding from comparing behavioral data to predictions from opsin distribution.

claim: The results suggest behavioral access to differential activation of rods and cones.
source: We find both wavelength-specific luminance and color contrast sensitivity to be dependent on retinotopic location, but that these differences in sensitivity were less dramatic than expected from the cone opsin distribution, suggesting behavioral access to differential activation of rods and cones.
evidence: Interpretation of the behavioral findings in relation to photoreceptor contributions.

claim: Total luminance was in the mesopic range (<3 cd/m2).
source: Total luminance was in the mesopic range (<3 cd/m2), over which mice are both behaviorally active (Daan et al., 2011) and color opponent signals have been demonstrated in the retina (Baden et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: Description of the experimental stimulus parameters.

claim: Mice are behaviorally active in the mesopic range.
source: Total luminance was in the mesopic range (<3 cd/m2), over which mice are both behaviorally active (Daan et al., 2011) and color opponent signals have been demonstrated in the retina (Baden et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on mouse behavioral activity.

claim: Color opponent signals have been demonstrated in the mouse retina in the mesopic range.
source: Total luminance was in the mesopic range (<3 cd/m2), over which mice are both behaviorally active (Daan et al., 2011) and color opponent signals have been demonstrated in the retina (Baden et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on retinal color opponent signals.

claim: Eye position did not change with stimulus location.
source: Eye position did not change with stimulus location (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Total luminance change detection saturated by ~30% at all elevations.
source: Total luminance change detection saturated by ~30% at all elevations (Figure 2A) and the half-saturation threshold (hereafter referred to as 'threshold') was less than 12% for each elevation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The half-saturation threshold for total luminance change detection was less than 12% for each elevation.
source: Total luminance change detection saturated by ~30% at all elevations (Figure 2A) and the half-saturation threshold (hereafter referred to as 'threshold') was less than 12% for each elevation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The highest luminance sensitivity was in the upper visual field, at 5.5% threshold.
source: The highest sensitivity was in the upper visual field, at 5.5% threshold, a threshold that is consistent with previous reports for a 15° (~0.07 cyc/°) stimulus (Histed et al., 2012; Prusky et al., 2000; Sinex et al., 1979; Umino et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to published literature.

claim: The 5.5% threshold is consistent with previous reports for a 15° stimulus.
source: The highest sensitivity was in the upper visual field, at 5.5% threshold, a threshold that is consistent with previous reports for a 15° (~0.07 cyc/°) stimulus (Histed et al., 2012; Prusky et al., 2000; Sinex et al., 1979; Umino et al., 2008).
evidence: Comparison of experimental findings to published literature.

claim: Sensitivity to increments in contrast was similar for all elevations (10.5–12.1%).
source: Sensitivity to increments in contrast was similar for all elevations (10.5–12.1%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Sensitivity to decrements in contrast was higher than sensitivity to increments.
source: Consistent with previous physiological measurements in V1 of mouse (Tan et al., 2015) and other species (Kremkow et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015), sensitivity to decrements in contrast was higher than sensitivity to increments (5.4%–10.4%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to published physiological studies.

claim: The difference between decrement and increment sensitivity was most pronounced in the upper visual field (5%) compared to the lower visual field (1.3%).
source: Notably, this was most pronounced in the upper visual field (difference: 5%) than the lower visual field (difference: 1.3%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Short wavelength band contrast sensitivity was non-uniform, with the highest sensitivity in the upper visual field (8% threshold).
source: For the short wavelength band (i.e. UV), contrast sensitivity was non-uniform, with the highest sensitivity in the upper visual field (Figure 2C,D; 8% threshold).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: For short-wavelength stimuli, mice were more sensitive to decrements than increments in contrast.
source: As with total luminance, mice were more sensitive to decrements than increments in contrast.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The non-uniformity across elevation was more pronounced for short-wavelength-specific sensitivity than total luminance, but was restricted to decrements.
source: The non-uniformity across elevation was more pronounced for short-wavelength-specific sensitivity than total luminance, but was restricted to decrements.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Middle-wavelength luminance contrast sensitivity was non-uniform across elevation, with higher sensitivity at the two lower elevations and the highest tested elevation.
source: The middle-wavelength (i.e. green) luminance contrast sensitivity was also non-uniform, across elevation, but with the opposite relationship as the short wavelength and total luminance: higher sensitivity at the two lower elevations and the highest tested elevation (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Middle-wavelength sensitivity was very similar for increments and decrements.
source: Middle-wavelength sensitivity was very similar for increments and decrements, again different than total and short-wavelength luminance contrast sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Luminance contrast sensitivity was non-uniform, with significant opposing wavelength-band-specific non-uniformities.
source: In summary, we found that luminance contrast sensitivity was non-uniform, with significant opposing wavelength-band-specific non-uniformities, although less than what would be predicted from the opsin expression or photoreceptor response alone, as shown below.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: The non-uniformities in luminance contrast sensitivity were less than what would be predicted from the opsin expression or photoreceptor response alone.
source: In summary, we found that luminance contrast sensitivity was non-uniform, with significant opposing wavelength-band-specific non-uniformities, although less than what would be predicted from the opsin expression or photoreceptor response alone, as shown below.
evidence: Comparison of experimental findings to predictions from opsin distribution.

claim: Mice were more sensitive to middle band stimulation than expected at all elevations tested.
source: We found the mouse to be more sensitive to middle band stimulation than expected at all elevations tested, including at 30° where, given the eye positioning (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), short-opsin expression dominates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data compared to predictions from opsin distribution.

claim: At 30° elevation, short-opsin expression dominates.
source: We found the mouse to be more sensitive to middle band stimulation than expected at all elevations tested, including at 30° where, given the eye positioning (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), short-opsin expression dominates.
evidence: Based on eye positioning data and established knowledge of opsin distribution.

claim: Mice were more sensitive to middle than short-band changes at all elevations.
source: In fact, surprisingly, the mice were more sensitive to middle than short-band changes at all elevations, with the following middle/short ratios: 3.4, 3.6, and 2.25 at –10°, 10°, and 30°, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The middle/short sensitivity ratio was 3.4 at -10° elevation.
source: In fact, surprisingly, the mice were more sensitive to middle than short-band changes at all elevations, with the following middle/short ratios: 3.4, 3.6, and 2.25 at –10°, 10°, and 30°, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The middle/short sensitivity ratio was 3.6 at 10° elevation.
source: In fact, surprisingly, the mice were more sensitive to middle than short-band changes at all elevations, with the following middle/short ratios: 3.4, 3.6, and 2.25 at –10°, 10°, and 30°, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The middle/short sensitivity ratio was 2.25 at 30° elevation.
source: In fact, surprisingly, the mice were more sensitive to middle than short-band changes at all elevations, with the following middle/short ratios: 3.4, 3.6, and 2.25 at –10°, 10°, and 30°, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The cone functional distribution predicts middle/short ratios of 2.3, 1.0, and 0.44 at –10°, 10°, and 30°, respectively.
source: Similar to the estimated relative opsin weights across V1 under photopic conditions (Aihara et al., 2017; Rhim et al., 2017), 2.3, 0.81, 0.81, the cone functional distribution predicts 2.3, 1.0, and 0.44 at –10°, 10°, and 30°, respectively.
evidence: Predictions based on published cone functional distribution data.

claim: Both cone opsin expression and cone functional distribution predict far less middle-band sensitivity than observed.
source: Both predict far less middle-band sensitivity that we observed.
evidence: Comparison of experimental findings to predictions from published data.

claim: Rod opsins contribute significantly to mouse perceptual sensitivity at mesopic light levels.
source: This result suggests that rod opsins, centered near the middle-band, contribute significantly to mouse perceptual sensitivity at these light levels, at least as much as 60% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) at higher elevations.
evidence: Interpretation of the discrepancy between observed and predicted sensitivity, supported by analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rod opsins may contribute at least as much as 60% to perceptual sensitivity at higher elevations.
source: This result suggests that rod opsins, centered near the middle-band, contribute significantly to mouse perceptual sensitivity at these light levels, at least as much as 60% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) at higher elevations.
evidence: Quantitative estimate based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Color discrimination was negligible at −10° elevation.
source: We found color discrimination to depend on elevation. Examining the adjusted data (Figure 3F–H), we found color discrimination was negligible at −10°, but mice were capable of varying levels of color sensitivity at all other elevations tested (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: Mice were capable of varying levels of color sensitivity at all elevations above -10°.
source: We found color discrimination to depend on elevation. Examining the adjusted data (Figure 3F–H), we found color discrimination was negligible at −10°, but mice were capable of varying levels of color sensitivity at all other elevations tested (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The performance along the equiluminant line at −10° was not well fit by a hyperbolic ratio function.
source: The performance along the equiluminant line at −10° was not well fit by a hyperbolic ratio function, and the performance in catch trials (0% contrast change, false-positive rate) was not significantly different from any point along the line (p>0.05, student's t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: At -10° elevation, performance in catch trials was not significantly different from any point along the equiluminant line.
source: The performance along the equiluminant line at −10° was not well fit by a hyperbolic ratio function, and the performance in catch trials (0% contrast change, false-positive rate) was not significantly different from any point along the line (p>0.05, student's t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Color contrast sensitivity was highest for decrements in short-middle opponency at 10° elevation (13.4%).
source: Color contrast sensitivity was highest for decrements in short-middle opponency at 10° elevation (13.4%); color sensitivity was nearly identical for decrements in short-middle opponent contrast at 30 and 50° and for increments at all elevations above the horizon (29.3–32.1%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Color sensitivity was nearly identical for decrements in short-middle opponent contrast at 30 and 50° and for increments at all elevations above the horizon (29.3–32.1%).
source: Color contrast sensitivity was highest for decrements in short-middle opponency at 10° elevation (13.4%); color sensitivity was nearly identical for decrements in short-middle opponent contrast at 30 and 50° and for increments at all elevations above the horizon (29.3–32.1%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The false-positive rate was markedly different between the lowest and other elevations.
source: Notably, the false-positive rate (0% contrast change, catch trials) was markedly different between the lowest and other elevations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The difference in false-positive rate is interpreted as a shift in strategy to maximize reward volume.
source: We interpret this is a shift in strategy in order to maximize reward volume, as the total volume of reward did not differ between −10° and the other elevations (0.8−0.92 mL/session, p>0.2, Welch's t-test), despite the lack of color discrimination at −10°.
evidence: Interpretation of the experimental findings based on reward volume analysis.

claim: Total volume of reward did not differ between −10° and the other elevations (0.8−0.92 mL/session, p>0.2).
source: We interpret this is a shift in strategy in order to maximize reward volume, as the total volume of reward did not differ between −10° and the other elevations (0.8−0.92 mL/session, p>0.2, Welch's t-test), despite the lack of color discrimination at −10°.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of reward volume data.

claim: Both wavelength-specific luminance and color contrast sensitivity is not uniform across the visual field, in accordance with the distributions of retinal and primary visual cortical responses.
source: The finding that both wavelength-specific luminance (Figure 2) and color contrast (Figure 3E–F) sensitivity is not uniform across the visual field is in accordance with the distributions of both retinal and primary visual cortical (Rhim et al., 2017) responses.
evidence: Comparison of experimental findings to published physiological data.

claim: Middle-band sensitivity was both higher and more uniform than expected.
source: However, we found that middle-band sensitivity was both higher and more uniform than expected (Figure 2).
evidence: Comparison of experimental findings to predictions.

claim: Rod sensitivity contributes significantly to perceptual sensitivity at mesopic light levels.
source: This suggests that rod sensitivity contributes significantly to perceptual sensitivity at these light levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Interpretation of the experimental findings supported by analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spatial scale of luminance and contrast adaptation can be large.
source: Because the spatial scale of luminance and contrast adaptation can be large (Smirnakis et al., 1997), the adaptation to large single-band stimuli (such as those produced by LCD or other sRGB displays) in these studies may underestimate the contrast sensitivity for cells in upper visual field.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on adaptation.

claim: Adaptation to large single-band stimuli may underestimate the contrast sensitivity for cells in upper visual field.
source: Because the spatial scale of luminance and contrast adaptation can be large (Smirnakis et al., 1997), the adaptation to large single-band stimuli (such as those produced by LCD or other sRGB displays) in these studies may underestimate the contrast sensitivity for cells in upper visual field.
evidence: Inference about potential experimental artifacts based on cited adaptation properties.

claim: Color sensitivity depends on retinotopy.
source: Our results also demonstrate that color sensitivity depends on retinotopy, and that some retinotopic locations appear to not support color discrimination.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: Some retinotopic locations appear to not support color discrimination.
source: Our results also demonstrate that color sensitivity depends on retinotopy, and that some retinotopic locations appear to not support color discrimination.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: Color-opponent cells are thought to underlie color discrimination behavior.
source: Because color-opponent cells, both single and double (Shapley and Hawken, 2011), are thought to underlie such behavior, our findings indicate that mice may have at least one, likely at least two, color-opponent cell types; the presence of such functional cell types may depend strongly on retinotopy.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on color-opponent cells.

claim: Mice may have at least one, likely at least two, color-opponent cell types.
source: Because color-opponent cells, both single and double (Shapley and Hawken, 2011), are thought to underlie such behavior, our findings indicate that mice may have at least one, likely at least two, color-opponent cell types; the presence of such functional cell types may depend strongly on retinotopy.
evidence: Inference from the experimental findings about color discrimination.

claim: The presence of color-opponent cell types may depend strongly on retinotopy.
source: Because color-opponent cells, both single and double (Shapley and Hawken, 2011), are thought to underlie such behavior, our findings indicate that mice may have at least one, likely at least two, color-opponent cell types; the presence of such functional cell types may depend strongly on retinotopy.
evidence: Inference from the experimental findings about retinotopic dependence of color discrimination.

claim: The animals are housed in an environment with fluorescent lighting that does not provide UV-B for reflection.
source: Notably, our animals are housed in an environment with fluorescent lighting that does not provide UV-B for reflection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the behavior we observed is developmentally specified, not learned, and further not lost through lack of use.
evidence: Description of housing conditions supported by spectral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The color discrimination behavior observed is developmentally specified, not learned.
source: Notably, our animals are housed in an environment with fluorescent lighting that does not provide UV-B for reflection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the behavior we observed is developmentally specified, not learned, and further not lost through lack of use.
evidence: Inference from the housing conditions and observed behavior.

claim: The color discrimination behavior is not lost through lack of use.
source: Notably, our animals are housed in an environment with fluorescent lighting that does not provide UV-B for reflection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the behavior we observed is developmentally specified, not learned, and further not lost through lack of use.
evidence: Inference from the housing conditions and observed behavior.

claim: Middle-wavelength opsin dominates the dorsal retina.
source: The distributions of cone opsins in the mouse retina has been well described, with only a subset of pure cones expressing only a single opsin and 40% of cones expressing a mix of both, and a non-uniform distribution of both pure and mixed cones: middle-wavelength opsin dominates the dorsal retina, although it also extends ventrally, while the short-wavelength opsin is more constrained to the ventral retina. (Applebury et al., 2000; Baden et al., 2013; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on opsin distribution.

claim: Middle-wavelength opsin extends ventrally in the mouse retina.
source: The distributions of cone opsins in the mouse retina has been well described, with only a subset of pure cones expressing only a single opsin and 40% of cones expressing a mix of both, and a non-uniform distribution of both pure and mixed cones: middle-wavelength opsin dominates the dorsal retina, although it also extends ventrally, while the short-wavelength opsin is more constrained to the ventral retina. (Applebury et al., 2000; Baden et al., 2013; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on opsin distribution.

claim: Short-wavelength opsin is more constrained to the ventral retina.
source: The distributions of cone opsins in the mouse retina has been well described, with only a subset of pure cones expressing only a single opsin and 40% of cones expressing a mix of both, and a non-uniform distribution of both pure and mixed cones: middle-wavelength opsin dominates the dorsal retina, although it also extends ventrally, while the short-wavelength opsin is more constrained to the ventral retina. (Applebury et al., 2000; Baden et al., 2013; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on opsin distribution.

claim: Only a subset of pure cones express only a single opsin.
source: The distributions of cone opsins in the mouse retina has been well described, with only a subset of pure cones expressing only a single opsin and 40% of cones expressing a mix of both, and a non-uniform distribution of both pure and mixed cones: middle-wavelength opsin dominates the dorsal retina, although it also extends ventrally, while the short-wavelength opsin is more constrained to the ventral retina. (Applebury et al., 2000; Baden et al., 2013; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on opsin expression.

claim: 40% of cones express a mix of both opsins.
source: The distributions of cone opsins in the mouse retina has been well described, with only a subset of pure cones expressing only a single opsin and 40% of cones expressing a mix of both, and a non-uniform distribution of both pure and mixed cones: middle-wavelength opsin dominates the dorsal retina, although it also extends ventrally, while the short-wavelength opsin is more constrained to the ventral retina. (Applebury et al., 2000; Baden et al., 2013; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on opsin expression.

claim: Cones are relatively uniform across the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina.
source: In total, cones are relatively uniform across the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina, although others report some increased density in the ventral retina.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with acknowledgment of some variation in reports.

claim: Some reports indicate increased cone density in the ventral retina.
source: In total, cones are relatively uniform across the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina, although others report some increased density in the ventral retina.
evidence: Reference to published reports on cone density.

claim: Rods are uniform across the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina.
source: Rods, on the other hand, are uniform across the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina and are much more numerous than cones (Jeon et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on rod distribution.

claim: Rods are much more numerous than cones.
source: Rods, on the other hand, are uniform across the dorsal-ventral axis of the retina and are much more numerous than cones (Jeon et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on photoreceptor numbers.

claim: If color responses rely only on cone signals they should follow the cone opsin distribution exactly.
source: If color responses, both physiological and behavioral, rely only on cone signals they should follow the cone opsin distribution exactly: more in the transition zone, some in the upper visual field, and none in the lower visual field.
evidence: Logical inference from the cone opsin distribution.

claim: The results are consistent with cone-cone opponency.
source: Our results are consistent with cone-cone opponency, as we observed a lack of color discrimination only in the lower visual field.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings in relation to cone opponency.

claim: The results indicate some rod-cone opponency.
source: However, our result also indicates some rod-cone opponency, as color change detection behavior thresholds relatively unchanged across 10° to 50°, despite the steep decline in middle opsin expression across this range of the retina (Baden et al., 2013).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings in relation to rod-cone opponency, supported by comparison to published opsin distribution data.

claim: Color change detection behavior thresholds are relatively unchanged across 10° to 50° elevation.
source: However, our result also indicates some rod-cone opponency, as color change detection behavior thresholds relatively unchanged across 10° to 50°, despite the steep decline in middle opsin expression across this range of the retina (Baden et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: There is a steep decline in middle opsin expression across 10° to 50° elevation in the retina.

claim: C57BL/6 mice can shift between diurnal, crepuscular, and nocturnal behavioral patterns over the course of the year.
source: Mice, while often considered nocturnal (Febinger et al., 2014), can be behaviorally active across a range of luminance conditions; C57BL/6 mice in particular can shift between diurnal, crepuscular, and nocturnal behavioral patterns over the course of the year (Daan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on mouse behavioral patterns.

claim: The results are consistent with the hypothesis that non-uniform wavelength-specific sensitivity is matched to the luminance statistics of natural scenes.
source: Our results are consistent with the hypothesis (Baden et al., 2013) that non-uniform wavelength-specific sensitivity is matched to the luminance statistics of natural scenes (UV in the upper visual field, green in the lower), and high sensitivity to decrements in the short wavelengths may be particularly helpful during the shift toward UV in the spectral radiance distribution the during twilight hours (Spitschan et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings in relation to published hypothesis and natural scene statistics.

claim: High sensitivity to decrements in the short wavelengths may be particularly helpful during twilight hours.
source: Our results are consistent with the hypothesis (Baden et al., 2013) that non-uniform wavelength-specific sensitivity is matched to the luminance statistics of natural scenes (UV in the upper visual field, green in the lower), and high sensitivity to decrements in the short wavelengths may be particularly helpful during the shift toward UV in the spectral radiance distribution the during twilight hours (Spitschan et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings in relation to twilight spectral radiance, supported by citation.

claim: The hypothesis that short-middle opponency is useful for identifying mouse urine posts is inconsistent with the lack of color discrimination at −10°.
source: Another hypothesis, that short-middle opponency is useful for identifying mouse urine posts (Joesch and Meister, 2016), is inconsistent with our demonstration of a lack of color discrimination at −10°, at least in absence of significant excursions in eye position or head movements.
evidence: Comparison of experimental findings to published hypothesis.

claim: Under mesopic conditions, color signals may be mediated by both cone-cone and some rod-cone opponency.
source: Our results suggest that, under the mesopic condition during which mice are often active, color signals may be mediated by both cone-cone and some rod-cone opponency, and this may facilitate the specialization of cone opsin distributions for sampling natural luminance statistics (Baden et al., 2013; Chiao et al., 2000).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings in relation to photoreceptor contributions and natural statistics.

claim: All animals used in this study were C57Bl/6J male mice aged 30–300 days.
source: All animals used in this study (n = 5) were C57Bl/6J male mice aged 30–300 days obtained from The Jackson Laboratories (IMSR_JAX:000664).

claim: A total of 127,659 trials were presented across all mice.
source: To achieve sufficient trials to cover this space, we presented a total of 127,659 trials (n = 4/5 total mice trained, 284 sessions).

claim: 44% of trials (56,112/127,659) were used for analysis after controlling for motivation.
source: To control for motivation, we calculated a running average of the reward rate and selected trials where this reward rate remained above four rewards per minute; only these engaged trials (44%; 56,112/127,659) were used for analysis.
evidence: Description of the data selection criteria and resulting dataset.
